definition.text: The science of finding the age of rocks, fossils and sediments from signatures held in the materials themselves.

facts.text: Absolute ages come from radioactive isotopes, while relative ages come from tools such as paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios.
Combining several dating indicators, including fossil-based ones, makes the recovered age more precise.
Radiometric dating measures how far an isotope of known half-life has decayed; slowly decaying isotopes reach further back but give less exact ages in years.
Radiocarbon dating suits organic samples younger than about 60,000 years, uranium–lead dating samples older than about 1 million years.
Uranium–thorium dating covers a few years to about 700,000 years and is used on speleothems, corals, carbonates and fossil bones.
Marker horizons are layers so distinctive that their age-equivalence across different sites is certain; dated volcanic ash layers are one example.
Incremental methods such as dendrochronology and lichenometry build year-by-year chronologies.
Amino acid dating is cheap but cannot give numerical ages without calibration from other methods at the same site.

title: Radiocarbon dating

definition.text: A method of finding the age of material containing organic carbon from how much of its radioactive carbon-14 is left.

facts.text: Cosmic rays striking atmospheric nitrogen constantly make carbon-14, which enters plants through photosynthesis and animals through the plants they eat.
When an organism dies it stops exchanging carbon and its carbon-14 decays, so older samples hold less of it.
Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,730 years, so reliable dates reach back to roughly 50,000 years ago.
Willard Libby developed the method at the University of Chicago in the late 1940s and received the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.
Dates must be corrected for fractionation and reservoir effects, and are complicated by fossil-fuel burning and 1950s–1960s nuclear tests.
Accelerator mass spectrometry counts every carbon-14 atom rather than only decays, so it works on samples as small as single seeds.
Contamination with 1% modern carbon makes a 17,000-year-old sample look 600 years younger; 1% old carbon makes any sample look about 80 years older.
Its impact on archaeology was so great that histories of the field call it the 'radiocarbon revolution'.

title: Radiocarbon calibration

definition.text: The use of a calibration curve of past atmospheric carbon-14 to convert a sample's radiocarbon measurement into an estimated calendar age.

facts.text: Calibration is needed because atmospheric carbon-14 has varied significantly, breaking the simple decay equation's assumption of a constant level.
Tree-ring sequences gave the first calibration data, and Hans Suess published the first calibration curve in 1967.
The IntCal curves, first published in 1998 and updated to 2020, have separate northern (IntCal20), southern (SHCal20) and marine (MARINE20) versions.
Uncalibrated 'conventional radiocarbon ages' still use the Libby half-life of 5568 years, agreed in 1962 for consistency with early papers.

distinct_from: Radiocarbon dating of soil and peat

title: Radiocarbon dating of soil and peat

definition.text: Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter in soils and peat, which is hard to do reliably because younger humic acid tends to contaminate it.

facts.text: For soil it is better to sieve out fragments of organic origin and date them with methods that tolerate small samples.
Of peat's humic acid, humins and fulvic acid, the humins give the most reliable date because they are insoluble in alkali and less contaminated.
Old carbon from limestone or groundwater can give apparent ages of thousands of years, and humus can do the same or, if younger, lower the apparent age.
Radiocarbon dating of soil organic carbon and lake methane showed 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon released over the last 60 years.

definition.text: The sudden rise of carbon-14 in Earth's atmosphere caused by above-ground nuclear tests from 1945 until the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty.

facts.text: The tests almost doubled the relative concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere.
Since the 1963 ban the relative concentration has fallen by about 4% a year, which lets scientists date recent tissues and deaths.
The pulse has been used to test atmospheric transport models and to study carbon movement between the atmosphere and oceanic or terrestrial sinks.
It will die out around 2030 if no more nuclear weapons are detonated above ground.

definition.text: A group of methods that find how long ago mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight or strong heating.

facts.text: Natural radiation from cosmic rays and traces of potassium, uranium, thorium and rubidium builds up trapped charge in buried quartz or feldspar grains.
Stimulating the grains with light or heat releases a luminescence signal whose intensity reflects how long they were buried.
The methods assume grains were 'bleached' when buried; 1–100 s of daylight resets quartz, as usually happens in dunes, loess and some water-laid deposits.
Age equals the equivalent dose in grays divided by the environmental dose rate, typically 0.5–5 Gy per 1000 years.
Quartz OSL ages typically span 100 to 350,000 years BP, with uncertainties of 5–10% of the age; feldspar IRSL may reach a million years.
Unlike radiocarbon dating it needs no organic material and avoids errors from old, carbon-14-deficient carbon.
At Lake Ulaan in Mongolia, wind-blown carbon from nearby soils and old carbonate rocks made radiocarbon dates up to 5800 years too old, while OSL was unaffected.
Thermoluminescence was first used to date unheated sediments in 1965, and optical dating with OSL was developed in 1984.

definition.text: A method of measuring the radiation dose a mineral has absorbed from the light it emits when stimulated, used to date sediments.

facts.text: Radiation traps electrons at impurities and defects in quartz and feldspar; light frees them, and they emit light when they recombine at luminescence centres.
Grains, usually coarse 100–200 μm or fine 4–11 μm, must be extracted from the sample without exposure to light.
It dates minerals rather than organic material, such as the deposition of wind-blown and river sediments.
Developed in 1984 by David J. Huntley and colleagues, it is now most often done by single-aliquot regeneration (SAR).

definition.text: Dating by the accumulated radiation dose of the time since crystalline material was last heated, as in lava or ceramics, or exposed to sunlight, as in sediments.

facts.text: Heating or sunlight empties the electron traps to zero; afterwards the surrounding radiation steadily refills them.
The dose measured by heating is divided by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays, to give the age.
The annual dose a buried object receives from the surrounding soil affects accuracy, so it is ideally measured at the find spot over a long period.
It is used where radiocarbon dating is not possible, such as for sediments; heated objects must have gone above 500 °C.

definition.text: A rare isotope created when a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus in the Solar System and knocks out protons and neutrons.

facts.text: They form within rocks and soil, in the atmosphere, and in meteoroids.
Useful ones are absent from the host material when it forms, so their build-up records later exposure.
Beryllium-10 (half-life 1,387,000 years) dates exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores; aluminium-26 and chlorine-36 date rocks and sediment.
In rock most of the cosmic-ray flux is absorbed within the first metre, where new nuclides form.
Spallation dominates in the top 0 to 60 cm, muon capture a few metres down, and neutron capture depends on snow, soil moisture and trace elements.
Air pressure changes nuclide production in minerals by a factor of 30 between sea level and the top of a 5 km mountain.

title: Surface exposure dating

definition.text: A set of techniques for estimating how long a rock has been exposed at or near Earth's surface.

facts.text: It dates glacial advances and retreats, erosion history, lava flows, rock slides and fault scarps, and works best for exposures of 10³ to 10⁶ years.
Measuring cosmogenic nuclide concentrations, with cosmic-ray flux and half-life, gives exposure time, burial time or how fast a drainage basin erodes.
Beryllium-10 and aluminium-26 form from quartz's oxygen and silicon; their ratio dates burial below the production depth, typically 2–10 meters.
Production rates are calibrated on samples dated by radiocarbon or luminescence, and the nuclides are measured by accelerator mass spectrometry.

definition.text: The use of beryllium-10, a cosmogenic isotope with a half-life of 1.387 million years formed in the atmosphere, to trace soil formation and erosion.

facts.text: Beryllium dissolves below about pH 5.5, so rain carries it down, and it drops out of solution as the water turns more alkaline.
It therefore accumulates at the soil surface, where its long half-life does not limit its residence time.
It has been used to study soil erosion, soil formation from regolith, the development of lateritic soils and the age of ice cores.
Short-lived beryllium-7, with a half-life of 53.22 days, shows that sediments are fresh, less than about 3–4 months old.

definition.text: The use of lead-210, a radioactive isotope in the uranium-238 decay chain with a half-life of 22.20 years, to date recent sediments and trace soil movement.

facts.text: Excess lead-210 from atmospheric fallout of radon-222 decay products builds up in surface soils.
Its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century, giving erosion and deposition rates and testing conservation practices.
Because its deposition is continuous and global, it complements the medium-term record from human-made radionuclides such as caesium-137.
It suits sedimentation chronologies on time scales shorter than 100 years.

title: δ13C

definition.text: A normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12, reported in parts per thousand (per mille, ‰).

facts.text: It compares a sample's 13C/12C ratio with that of an established reference standard, expressed per mille.
The original standard, a Cretaceous belemnite fossil (PDB), ran out and was replaced by standards such as VPDB.
Organisms take up light carbon-12 preferentially and have δ13C of about −25‰, depending on their metabolic pathway.
C4 plants have δ13C of −16 to −10‰ and C3 plants −33 to −24‰, so the rise of C4 grasses can be traced through time.
It separates carbon dioxide from ecosystem respiration from that of burned fossil fuels, the basis of the Suess effect.
Carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules of paleosols are used to reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide.
On the Loess Plateau, δ13C of pedogenic carbonate rose by 5% over the Late Miocene and Pliocene, indicating drying.

notes: S:f8aa8c8fee13 gives the Loess Plateau δ13C changes in % (2.5% and 5%); probably per mille in the original, kept as stated.

definition.text: The study of acid-resistant microscopic organic remains, such as pollen and spores, found in sediments and sedimentary rocks.

facts.text: Palynomorphs, 5 to 500 micrometres across, include pollen, spores, dinoflagellate cysts, fungi and plant tissue.
They are extracted from soils, rocks and sediment cores by ultrasonic treatment, wet sieving and acid digestion that remove the mineral fraction.
Potassium hydroxide removes humic substances, hydrofluoric acid digests silicate minerals, and acetolysis dissolves the cellulose that hampers work on peat.
Quantitative pollen analysis began with Lennart von Post, whose 1916 Kristiania lecture spread the method.
Grains of each taxon are counted under the microscope to make a pollen diagram, with depth on the y-axis and abundance on the x-axis.
Records from peat or lake sediments reconstruct past vegetation and climate and reveal human effects such as logging and land use.
It is applied in geology, archaeology, pedology and physical geography, including relative dating of strata through biostratigraphy.

definition.text: An organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or fossil soils (paleosols).

facts.text: Rhizoliths include root moulds, casts, tubules, petrifactions and rhizocretions.
They help identify paleosols, but only in post-Silurian beds, since plants with extensive roots did not flourish before then.
Roots that secrete bicarbonate rather than hydrogen ions raise the surrounding pH, which may trigger calcium carbonate to precipitate as rhizocretions.
Rhizohaloes are grey reduced zones with reddish rims around decayed roots; rhizolith mineralogy shows how waterlogged a paleosol was.

title: Silurian-Devonian Terrestrial Revolution

definition.text: The rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago, in the Silurian and Devonian periods.

facts.text: Earlier non-vascular plants lacked the deep roots needed to break solid rock into regolith and soil.
Plant roots eroded rock and created a water-holding, mineral- and organic-rich soil layer, the pedosphere.
Roots and their microbial partners formed the rhizosphere, speeding weathering and releasing phosphates, calcium and magnesium, as pedogenic carbonates show.
Enhanced silicate weathering is thought to have cut atmospheric CO2 from around 6300 to 2100 ppmv, though another hypothesis says plants slowed weathering.

contested_note: Sources disagree whether early land plants increased silicate weathering or instead lowered CO2 mainly through organic carbon burial in wetlands.

definition.text: Dating and correlating sequences and events by their position between layers of volcanic ash (tephra) of known date.

facts.text: Each eruption leaves a tephra horizon with a unique chemical fingerprint, which becomes a time marker once the eruption is dated.
Ash falls almost instantly over wide areas, linking distant sequences into one 'age-equivalent' chronology and checking other dating methods.
Fingerprinting uses the electron microprobe and laser-ablation ICP-MS on single shards, though basaltic tephra chemistry can alter over time.
Since the late 1990s, invisible 'cryptotephra' layers have been extracted from archives such as peat, lake sediment and loess.
